title: Stack selection
description: Which agentic stack fits your context: Claude Code, Sovereign, Cloud-OSS or Behind-GFW

objectives.text: Break an agentic stack down into three layers (agent/UI, routing/gateway, model provider) and explain that each layer is swapped independently
Choose one of the four stacks based on your constraints (budget, access, hardware, privacy, setup time) and name the trade-offs of that choice
Explain what the LiteLLM gateway gives you and how the fallback chain works all the way down to the local “floor”
Tell the boss-worker scheme (Hermes) apart from a single agent that does everything itself, and determine when it's justified
Draw up a step-by-step migration plan in which the old stack stays as a fallback until the new one has been tested on a real task

checks.question: The combination “Claude Code → LiteLLM → Cerebras gpt-oss-120b” from the lesson shows the main property of a stack. Which one?
options: Each layer (agent, gateway, provider) can be swapped independently of the others
Claude Code works only with Anthropic models
A gateway is required only for Chinese models
The agent and the model are the same thing; you choose them together
checks.explain: A stack in the course consists of three layers, and each is replaced separately. That's why you can keep the convenient Claude Code interface and connect an open model to it (u1, “What ‘stack’ means here”).

checks.question: Your company forbids sending code to an outside vendor. Which of the Claude Code drawbacks named in the lesson settles the matter here?
options: A minimum of ~$20 a month
It needs a discrete graphics card
Telemetry: every request goes to Anthropic
It only works on a Mac
checks.explain: Of the four drawbacks (price, access, vendor lock-in, telemetry), telemetry is the one that bears on a ban on sharing code. The lesson doesn't name a graphics card or a Mac as Claude Code requirements (u1, “Why not ‘just Claude Code’”).

checks.question: You're not in China, your budget is $0, and all you have is a laptop without a GPU. Where does the lesson's decision tree lead?
options: Claude Code
Cloud-OSS
Sovereign
Behind-GFW
checks.explain: The first fork — China — gives “no.” There's no $20+ budget. There's no GPU or Mac M-series either. That leaves Cloud-OSS (u2, “Decision tree (if still unsure)”).

checks.question: What do you pay for the maximum privacy of the Sovereign stack?
options: The highest subscription price
It doesn't work in China
Being tied to a single vendor
The longest setup (half a day) and slightly lower out-of-box quality
checks.explain: In the trade-offs table, Sovereign has maximum privacy and no vendor lock-in, but setup takes half a day, and out-of-box quality is 7/10 versus 9/10 for Claude Code (u2, “Honest trade-offs”).

checks.question: What does the LiteLLM gateway change for the agent when there are several providers underneath it?
options: The agent has to switch between provider addresses in turn
The gateway writes the code itself instead of the agent
The agent sees a single endpoint, and the gateway takes care of switching between providers on failure
The gateway is only needed to make things free
checks.explain: In the lesson's image, the gateway is the conductor. The agent calls a single point, and under the hood the gateway distributes requests and moves on to fallback models (u2, reflection).

checks.question: The lesson's config sets `fast-pool: ["balanced", "local-floor"]`. What happens if Cerebras (`fast-pool`) stops responding?
options: The agent returns an error, and the request has to be repeated by hand
The gateway waits until Cerebras comes back
The request goes to paid Anthropic
The gateway sends the request to `balanced` (Gemini), and if that fails too — to the local model
checks.explain: `fallbacks` records the order of the fallback options: Gemini first (in China, a Chinese provider), the local llama-server last. There's no Anthropic in this config at all (u3, step 3).

checks.question: Why put a local model on llama-server at the end of the chain if the clouds are faster?
options: It's the “floor” for when all the clouds are unavailable at once
A local model is always smarter than cloud ones
LiteLLM won't start without a local model
The clouds forbid using them without a local model
checks.explain: The local model is the last level: it works even when not a single cloud responds. Its speed is more modest, but it depends neither on the network nor on someone else's limits (u3, step 4).

checks.question: LiteLLM is already running on `localhost:4000`. You want to try Cline instead of Aider. What will you have to change?
options: The whole LiteLLM config and the provider keys
Only the agent's connection: point it at the same `localhost:4000` and the model name
Move to a different model provider, because Cline doesn't work with Cerebras
Set up a separate gateway for each agent
checks.explain: The gateway serves an OpenAI-compatible API. Any such agent connects to it the same way, so switching agents touches neither the gateway nor the providers (u3, step 5).

checks.question: An agent is refactoring a module; by the fifth file it forgets the original plan and spends a lot of tokens getting back to it. How does the Hermes scheme answer this problem?
options: It gives the agent a model with a bigger window so everything fits
The boss holds only the plan and state, and hands the implementation to workers — narrow subtasks with their own context
It forbids refactoring across several files
It runs all the workers with a shared context so each one sees everything
checks.explain: This is the context-saturation pattern: one agent tries to play every role. Hermes works as a director: it frames a subtask, hands it to a worker, checks the result, and updates the plan. Implementation doesn't eat its context (u4, reflection).

checks.question: For which task is the boss-worker scheme most likely unnecessary?
options: A small edit in a single file
Several days of work on a long plan
Regular scheduled tasks (cron)
A big plan that has to be handed out to several workers
checks.explain: The lesson calls boss-worker overkill for small tasks. It pays off on long plans, multi-day work, and cron tasks (u4, practice).

checks.question: You've chosen a new stack. Which move does the lesson call the most common migration mistake?
options: Keeping both stacks running in parallel for a week
Moving one real task over first
Writing down where the new stack is slower and where it's faster
Deleting the old tool right away and switching completely to the new one
checks.explain: The lesson compares migration to shedding a skin: the new stack first grows over the old one, and for a while both work. The other options are exactly the steps of the recommended plan (u5, reflection).

checks.question: Why, on the second day of the plan, repeat on the new stack a task you've already solved on the old one?
options: To get a second, better result for that task
To convince yourself that the new one is better
To compare the stacks on a familiar task and record facts: where it's slower, where it's faster, where the problems are
To delete the old stack right after that
checks.explain: A familiar task is a fair yardstick: the result is already known, and you see the difference that comes from the stack itself. The template asks you to record facts, not to talk yourself into anything (u5, “Migration template”).
